Abstract
We review recent experimental progress towards quantum information processing and quantum
simulation using neutral atoms in two-dimensional (2D) arrays of optical microtraps as 2D registers
of qubits. We describe a scalable quantum information architecture based on micro-fabricated
optical elements, simultaneously targeting the important issues of single-site addressability and
scalability. This approach provides ﬂexible and integrable conﬁgurations for quantum state storage,
manipulation, and retrieval. We present recent experimental results on the initialization and
coherent one-qubit rotation of up to 100 individually addressable qubits, the coherent transport of
atomic quantum states in a scalable quantum shift register, and discuss the feasibility of two-qubit
gates in 2D microtrap arrays.

Quantum Darwinism demonstrates not only that preferred states are selected for their stability but also that information about them is broadcast by the same environment that causes decoherence and einselection. That environment acts both as a censor and as an advertising agent that disseminates information about pointer states while suppressing complementary information. Chapter 8 explores the implications and limitations of quantum Darwinism using models inspired by the structure of the Universe we inhabit. We perceive our Universe using light and other means of information transmission. We explore models that have a well-defined relation with our everyday reality, and where one can also selectively relax some of the idealized assumptions and investigate the consequences. Light is the communication channel through which we obtain most of our information. Fortunately, it is an ideal channel in the sense of quantum Darwinism, and simple but realistic cases are exactly solvable. Decomposition-Indexed Classicality: An A/R/F Framework for Observer-Dependent Quantum Experience
Authors/Creators
Almon, Ricardo
(Producer)

Producer:

Description
This work develops a quantitative framework for
observer-dependent classicality
in quantum mechanics based on three operational functionals:
Redundancy (R)
,
Accessibility (A)
, and
Observer Flow (F)
. The A/R/F framework distinguishes environmental redundancy from the effective redundancy usable by a specific observer, models accessibility through a noisy-threshold aperture function, and introduces a continuity measure governing an observer’s capacity to integrate records over time. Classicality becomes a
decomposition-indexed property
, not a global feature of the universal wavefunction.
Applied to
Wigner’s Friend
and
Frauchiger–Renner
, the framework dissolves paradoxes by showing that cross-agent inferences fail precisely in regimes where effective accessibility is low. The paper outlines experimental signatures, including observer-dependent classicality thresholds and flow-disruption tests, offering a route toward
empirical constraints on observer-relative quantum structure
.

Title:
Perfect Sampling for (Atomic) Lovász Local Lemma
Authors:
Kun He
,
Xiaoming Sun
,
Kewen Wu
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
We give a Markov chain based perfect sampler for uniform sampling solutions of constraint satisfaction problems (CSP). Under some mild Lovász local lemma conditions where each constraint of the CSP has a small number of forbidden local configurations, our algorithm is accurate and efficient: it outputs a perfect uniform random solution and its expected running time is quasilinear in the number of variables. Prior to our work, perfect samplers are only shown to exist for CSPs under much more restrictive conditions (Guo, Jerrum, and Liu, JACM'19).
Our algorithm has two components:
1. A simple perfect sampling algorithm using bounding chains (Huber, STOC'98; Haggstrom and Nelander, Scandinavian Journal of Statistics'99). This sampler is efficient if each variable domain is small.
2. A simple but powerful state tensorization trick to reduce large domains to smaller ones. This trick is a generalization of state compression (Feng, He, and Yin, STOC'21).
The crux of our analysis is a simple information percolation argument which allows us to achieve bounds even beyond current best approximate samplers (Jain, Pham, and Vuong, ArXiv'21).
Previous related works either use intricate algorithms or need sophisticated analysis or even both. Thus we view the simplicity of both our algorithm and analysis as a strength of our work.
